question: A 2-week-old infant is brought to the physician by her father because of a 1-week history of vaginal discharge. The discharge was initially clear, but now he notices that it is tinged with blood. The father is also concerned about “bruises” on his daughter's back and buttocks. Both parents work so that the infant spends most of her time in daycare or with her aunt. She was born at term following a pregnancy complicated by maternal gonococcal infection that was treated with antibiotics. She appears well. Physical examination shows mild acne across her cheeks and forehead. There are multiple large flat gray-blue patches on her back and buttocks. An image of one of the lesions is shown. Firm breast buds are present. Genitourinary examination shows erythema and swelling of the vulva and vagina with an odorless, blood-stained white discharge. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Maternal gonococcal infection during pregnancy -> possible vertical transmission to the infant -> genital infection in the infant -> vaginal discharge with blood tinge -> 70% confidence. CHAIN: Presence of large flat gray-blue patches on back and buttocks -> possible Mongolian spots -> common in infants of color -> benign finding -> 80% confidence. CHAIN: Firm breast buds present -> normal physiological finding in newborns -> due to maternal hormones -> 90% confidence. CHAIN: Genitourinary examination shows erythema and swelling of vulva and vagina -> possible infection or inflammation -> further evaluation needed -> 70% confidence. CHAIN: Mild acne across cheeks and forehead -> common in newborns due to maternal hormones -> benign finding -> 80% confidence. CHAIN: Next step in management -> further evaluation of the genital infection and consideration of appropriate therapy -> 70%
analysis: The infant's presentation with vaginal discharge, blood-stained discharge, and genital findings raises concern for precocious puberty. The large flat gray-blue patches on the back and buttocks are consistent with Mongolian spots, which are benign birthmarks. Given the history of maternal gonococcal infection, the infant should be evaluated for possible sexual abuse. The most appropriate next step would be to conduct a thorough evaluation for sexual abuse, including appropriate laboratory tests and involving child protective services.
